title: Orléans Heresy Trials: First Burning of Christian Heretics in the West
description: In 1022 CE at Orléans, fourteen canons of the cathedral were tried before King Robert II of France and burned as heretics — the first judicial execution of Christian heretics in the medieval West. Contemporary accounts by Adémar de Chabannes and Paul of Chartres described the accused as practicing secret nocturnal meetings, invoking demons, engaging in sexual license, and worshipping a being who appeared as a black man or dark spirit. Whether these descriptions reflected actual beliefs, judicial projection, or both remains debated, but the Orléans case established a template connecting heresy with diabolical worship, secret meetings, and sexual transgression that would be elaborated over the following centuries. This early association between heresy and diabolic practice was a crucial step toward the fully developed witchcraft stereotype.
historiographical_note: R.I. Moore's The Formation of a Persecuting Society (1987) situates the Orléans burnings in a broader pattern of institutionalized persecution developing in eleventh-century Europe. Norman Cohn's Europe's Inner Demons argues that such heresy accusations were largely projections by authorities rather than descriptions of actual practices, a view contested by historians who find evidence of genuine heterodox movements.
source_method: Adémar de Chabannes chronicle; Paul of Chartres account; secondary scholarship on eleventh-century heresy
